objective: Write a hardened container securityContext: runAsNonRoot, readOnlyRootFilesystem, allowPrivilegeEscalation false, dropped capabilities, no privileged or host namespaces
secondaryObjectives: Use appropriate Pod Security Standards: apply the privileged, baseline and restricted profiles through Pod Security Admission namespace labels and fix workloads that fail them
Manage Kubernetes Secrets securely: encryption at rest with an EncryptionConfiguration, RBAC on secrets, mounting over environment variables, and external secret stores

Read 2026-11-17 with WebFetch (a summarizing fetch) of the primary page, found by WebSearch. Confirms: enforce rejects Pods that violate the level; audit adds an audit annotation; warn returns a user-facing warning; restrictions apply when Pods are created; audit and warn also check workload resources, enforce only the resulting Pods.

sources.cite: Kubernetes documentation, Enforce Pod Security Standards with Namespace Labels
sources.note: Read 2026-11-17 with WebFetch (a summarizing fetch) of the primary page, found by WebSearch. Confirms: namespaces are labeled pod-security.kubernetes.io/<mode>=<level>; kubectl label --dry-run=server shows how a new level would treat existing Pods without changing the policy.

Read 2026-11-17 with WebFetch (a summarizing fetch) of the primary page, found by WebSearch. Confirms: the Restricted profile requires allowPrivilegeEscalation false, runAsNonRoot true, runAsUser not 0, a seccomp profile of RuntimeDefault or Localhost, and dropping ALL capabilities (only NET_BIND_SERVICE may be added); readOnlyRootFilesystem is not part of the profile (the case adds it as further hardening).

sources.cite: Kubernetes documentation, Good practices for Kubernetes Secrets (v1.34)
sources.note: Read 2026-11-17 with WebFetch (a summarizing fetch) of the primary page, found by WebSearch. Confirms: Secrets are stored unencrypted in etcd by default and encryption at rest should be configured; get, watch and list on Secrets should be restricted, and list access implicitly reveals Secret contents.

The company, the clusters, the workloads and the people are fictional. The minutes or days each step takes and the effects of each decision are teaching simplifications for exam practice, not measured values.

brief.situation: You are the Kubernetes security engineer at Cobaltline Payments, a fictional card processor. A penetration test found the payments-api container running as root with privilege escalation allowed and its database password in an environment variable. The audit wants the namespace on the restricted Pod Security Standard by Friday.
handover: The payments namespace has no Pod Security Admission labels.
payments-api: runs as root, writable root filesystem, all default capabilities, DB_PASSWORD in env from a Secret.
howItWorks: The terminal shows each command's output; the map shows each component and its status in words.
Move on a check-in at a time. A decision comes to you at each check-in; before the first, you can read the evidence.
At the end you write the record and a short reflection.

then.log: Check-in 2: a node is drained early for the upgrade; payments-api's replacement Pods are rejected by admission and card payments fail.
Check-in 3: the pentesters return through the same bug; from the privileged container they mount the node's filesystem and read every Pod's secrets on it.
Check-in 4: a read-only monitoring role, which can read ConfigMaps, exposes the database password in its dashboard.

effects.log: Check-in 2: the payments team asks what the container needs.

psaPrompt.title: Turn on the restricted profile
psaPrompt.context: Two workloads would fail restricted today. A node pool upgrade tonight will reschedule every Pod.

choices.label: Label the namespace warn=restricted and audit=restricted now, fix the two workloads, then add enforce=restricted once the dry run is clean

effects.log: warn and audit are on; enforce waits for clean workloads.

choices.feedback: warn and audit show violations without rejecting Pods; enforce comes once the workloads pass.

choices.label: Enforce baseline now and leave restricted for next quarter
choices.feedback: baseline blocks the worst (privileged, host namespaces) but allows root and privilege escalation, which is what the pentest found.

choices.label: Label enforce=restricted right away to meet the audit
choices.feedback: Running Pods stay, but every new Pod of the two workloads is rejected: tonight's node upgrade will leave them with none.

ctxPrompt.title: Harden payments-api
ctxPrompt.context: The app needs no capabilities, writes only /tmp and listens on 8080.

choices.label: runAsNonRoot true with a non-zero runAsUser, readOnlyRootFilesystem true with an emptyDir at /tmp, allowPrivilegeEscalation false, capabilities drop ALL, seccompProfile RuntimeDefault

effects.log: The container runs hardened and passes restricted.

choices.feedback: Each setting removes something an attacker inside the container could use, and together they meet restricted.

choices.label: Set runAsNonRoot only
choices.feedback: A good start, but privilege escalation, capabilities and seccomp still fail restricted.

choices.label: Set privileged: true so the debugging sidecar keeps working, and exempt the namespace

effects.log: The container is privileged and the namespace exempted.

choices.feedback: A privileged container is the host: an attacker in it can escape to the node.

secPrompt.title: The password in an environment variable
secPrompt.context: The password is injected as DB_PASSWORD. Three service accounts can list Secrets in the namespace. etcd encryption at rest is not configured.

choices.label: Mount the Secret as a read-only file, remove get and list on Secrets from the three service accounts, and enable an EncryptionConfiguration for Secrets at rest

effects.log: The password is a mounted file; RBAC is narrowed; Secrets are encrypted at rest.

choices.feedback: A mounted file is not in the process environment, fewer identities can read it, and etcd no longer holds it in plain text.

choices.label: Mount the Secret as a file and leave RBAC and etcd for later

effects.log: The password is a mounted file.

choices.feedback: Better, but three service accounts can still read it and etcd stores it in plain text.

choices.label: Move the password into a ConfigMap so it is not 'a Secret' any more

effects.log: The password moves into a ConfigMap.

choices.feedback: ConfigMaps are readable far more widely than Secrets and are never encrypted at rest.

reflection.question: Write the change record for the audit: how the restricted profile was rolled out, what the hardened container sets, and how the password is protected.

parts.label: Profile and container
parts.criteria: warn and audit first, then enforce; the full hardened securityContext with an emptyDir for /tmp.
parts.modelAnswer: We labeled warn and audit restricted, fixed both workloads, then enforced. payments-api runs as non-root with a read-only root, no escalation, all capabilities dropped and RuntimeDefault seccomp.

parts.label: The Secret
parts.criteria: Mounted as a file, RBAC narrowed, EncryptionConfiguration for Secrets.
parts.modelAnswer: The password is a mounted file, only payments-api's account can read it, and Secrets are encrypted at rest.

scoring.modelReasoning: Pod Security Admission applies the Pod Security Standards per namespace by label: enforce rejects new Pods that fail, while warn and audit only report, so roll a stricter profile out with warn and audit, fix the workloads, then enforce. The restricted profile needs non-root, no privilege escalation, all capabilities dropped and a seccomp profile; a read-only root filesystem with an emptyDir for scratch space removes write access an attacker would use. Secrets are safer mounted as files, readable by as few identities as possible and encrypted at rest with an EncryptionConfiguration.
